The paper investigates the time-dependent, non-equilibrium thermal and ionization history of gas cooling radiatively from 10^6 K.
The model uses a one-dimensional, planar, steady-state flow model of the galactic fountain.
The initial flow velocity was ~100 km/s, comparable to the sound speed of 10^6 K gas.
The initial density was n_H,0 ~2x10^-2 cm^-3, in reasonable agreement with other observational estimates.
The new calculations that include radiative transfer allow for a much larger range of cooling region sizes, up to D ≤ 0.15 pc, compared to the previous limit of D ≤ 1 kpc.
Self-ionization was found to be sufficient to cause the flow to match the observed galactic halo column densities and UV emission.
For the case with v_0 = 100 km/s and n_H,0 = 2x10^-2 cm^-3, the cooling region size was found to be D ~40 pc.
The model also compared predicted Ha fluxes, UV line emission, and broadband X-ray fluxes with observed values.
One-dimensional numerical hydrodynamical calculations including the effects of radiative cooling were also presented.
The left panel of Fig. 1 shows the predicted column density ratios N(N V)/N(C IV), N(Si IV)/N(C IV), and N(O VI)/N(C IV) as a function of (n_H,0 * t).
The right panel of Fig. 1 shows the temperature and log(10^7 * N(C IV)) evolution during the radiative cooling process.
The observed range for the column density ratios is indicated by vertical bars in the left panel of Fig. 1.
The paper demonstrates the importance of self-ionization in enabling the galactic fountain model to match observational data.
The new calculations that include radiative transfer confirm the importance of self-ionization but allow for a much larger range of cooling region sizes.
The model provides insights into the thermal and ionization history of gas in the galactic fountain.
